title: Francis Fukuyama takes stock
gist: In an interview timed to his new memoir 'In the Realm of the Last Man,' Francis Fukuyama argues Trump is trying to make America authoritarian but will likely be checked by a 'big pushback' in the 2026 midterms and a broader global reversal of populist-nationalist forces (Orbán's ousting, Putin's battlefield struggles), while warning the bigger long-term risk is a 'generational cycle' in which populations with no memory of dictatorship (e.g. Poland) drift toward illiberalism out of boredom or resentment of 'Brussels.'

insights.claim: Fukuyama says he is confident there will be 'a big pushback' against Republican rule in the autumn 2026 US midterm elections, framing this as part of a broader global pattern of pushback against populist-nationalist forces, alongside Viktor Orbán's recent ousting in Hungary and Putin's increasing difficulties on the Ukraine battlefield.
insights.speaker: Francis Fukuyama
insights.so_what: A specific, near-dated (autumn 2026) political prediction that can be checked against midterm results; a Republican setback would be consistent with Fukuyama's broader 'populist reversal' thesis relevant to US policy-continuity risk pricing.
insights.quote: confident that there will be a big pushback

insights.claim: Fukuyama is far more worried about the 2028 US presidential race than the 2026 midterms, fearing Democrats 'living in cloud cuckoo land' could nominate a candidate who could win in New York or San Francisco but 'just cannot win nationwide.'
insights.speaker: Francis Fukuyama
insights.so_what: Signals elevated risk that Democratic primary dynamics could produce a general-election-weak nominee in 2028, a factor relevant to modeling continuity/discontinuity of US federal policy beyond Trump's term.
insights.quote: could win in New York or San Francisco... but just cannot win nationwide.

insights.claim: Fukuyama predicts Germany's AfD may come to power in one or two German states, calling this 'a big precedent,' but expects the country's proportional voting system to force any AfD-involved government to operate within serious coalition constraints; he similarly predicts Marine Le Pen could win the French presidency in 2027 but would likely have to govern within EU- and Nato-compliant constraints similar to Giorgia Meloni's Italy rather than following Orbán's more unilateral model.
insights.speaker: Francis Fukuyama
insights.so_what: Distinguishes between headline populist-right electoral wins and their actual policy latitude once in office -- useful for calibrating how much market/policy disruption to price in even if AfD or Le Pen win power, versus assuming Orbán-style unconstrained rule.
insights.locator: paragraph on AfD and Le Pen

themes.theme: The 'generational cycle' thesis on liberal democracy

insights.claim: Fukuyama's central revised thesis is that the 'end of history' may be 'a sort of cyclical thing' where societies periodically experiment with illiberal solutions, learn how bad they are, and cycle back to liberal democracy -- driven by the fact that 'one of the most powerful drivers of belief in liberalism is to live in an illiberal society,' meaning populations without direct experience of dictatorship (e.g. Poland) become susceptible to believing 'Brussels is the real dictatorship.'
insights.speaker: Francis Fukuyama
insights.so_what: A generational, cyclical (not linear/permanent) model of democratic backsliding implies markets should expect recurring populist waves roughly once per generation in stable democracies rather than either permanent liberal consolidation or permanent authoritarian capture -- relevant to long-horizon political-risk allocation.
insights.quote: one of the most powerful drivers of belief in liberalism is to live in an illiberal society... the 'end of history' is going to be a sort of cyclical thing, where we are going to have to go through periods of experimenting with illiberal solutions to this longing for an alternative, and then learn how bad they are, and then go back to accepting liberal democracy.

insights.claim: Contrary to what the interviewer expected, Fukuyama says the biggest change in his thinking is not driven by wage stagnation or inequality in Western economies -- he maintains liberal democracy still provides 'objective material conditions that have never been better' -- but by this generational/psychological cycle of forgetting why liberalism was valued.
insights.speaker: Francis Fukuyama
insights.so_what: A direct pushback against the dominant 'economic anxiety drives populism' narrative from one of the field's most cited political theorists -- implies policy responses focused solely on redistribution/inequality may not address the actual driver of democratic backsliding.
insights.quote: objective material conditions that have never been better
insights.locator: paragraph on what has changed for Fukuyama

insights.claim: Fukuyama's original 1989 'end of history' thesis (expanded in 1992) explicitly predicted this backlash: he wrote then that 'the end of history will be a very sad time' because it would leave no outlet for 'daring, courage, imagination and idealism,' and used Nietzsche's 'last man' concept to warn that human appetite for dominance or boredom could turn people against liberal democracy -- a prediction he now says has been vindicated by the populist wave.
insights.speaker: Francis Fukuyama
insights.so_what: Establishes that Fukuyama's most-cited caveat (largely ignored by his critics, per the article's framing) already anticipated today's populist backlash 30+ years in advance -- relevant context for weighting his current predictions as having a strong track record on this specific dynamic.
insights.quote: the end of history will be a very sad time
insights.locator: paragraph on 1992 book and Nietzsche's 'last man'

themes.theme: Critique of reductive analytical frameworks in economics and IR

insights.claim: Fukuyama argues mainstream economics' atomistic, self-interest-based models cannot be adequately fixed by adding 'altruism,' 'habit,' or other nonmaterial preferences as tweaks, because once you account for people wanting things for others the way they want things for themselves, models will 'obviously have trouble predicting' anything at all.
insights.speaker: Francis Fukuyama
insights.so_what: A structural critique of standard rational-choice economic modeling from a political scientist -- reinforces the case for behavioral/institutional approaches over narrow utility-maximization models when forecasting real-world economic behavior.

insights.claim: Fukuyama draws a direct parallel between economists reducing people to 'utility' maximizers and realist international-relations theorists treating states as 'impenetrable billiard balls' whose behavior is explained by an ill-defined 'national interest' without examining the internal politics that actually determine what that interest is judged to be.
insights.speaker: Francis Fukuyama
insights.so_what: A reusable analytical framework for geopolitical forecasting: treating 'national interest' as endogenously shaped by domestic politics (not a fixed external variable) implies analysts should track internal political coalitions, not just stated geopolitical doctrine, to predict state behavior (e.g. on Russia, Iran, China).

themes.theme: Personal history shaping his political evolution

insights.claim: Fukuyama broke publicly with his neoconservative circle over the Iraq War only in 2004 (not during the 2002-03 buildup, despite having signed a letter calling for Saddam Hussein's removal), concluding the failure was not conspiracy but a 'practical' failure to think through consequences -- and says he sees Trump making 'the same maddening mistake' in Iran today.
insights.speaker: Francis Fukuyama
insights.so_what: Fukuyama explicitly maps his own critique of the 2003 Iraq intervention onto current Trump policy toward Iran, positioning him as a likely skeptical voice on any escalation of US action against Iran -- useful for gauging elite foreign-policy establishment sentiment on Iran risk.
insights.quote: sometimes it takes an extremely intelligent person to convince themselves of something implausible.

insights.claim: Fukuyama rejects racial identity politics as 'foolish,' saying it 'confines you to an ethnic ghetto' rather than allowing full assimilation, drawing on his own family's experience of Japanese-American internment during WWII (during which his grandfather's Los Angeles hardware store was lost) followed by his father's full academic assimilation via a Nebraska college scholarship.
insights.speaker: Francis Fukuyama
insights.so_what: Reveals a consistent, decades-long ideological throughline (pro-assimilation, anti-identity-politics) that predates and explains his more recent public disagreements with progressive cultural politics -- relevant context for interpreting his stance on future US culture-war debates.
insights.quote: it confines you to an ethnic ghetto, if you don't just think of you as an American.
